posts.title: PagedAttention: OS Memory Tricks for LLM Serving
posts.subtitle: How vLLM stopped wasting 70% of your GPU's KV cache
posts.summary: PagedAttention borrows virtual memory's paging trick to manage the KV cache: instead of reserving one giant contiguous block per request, it stores keys/values in small fixed-size blocks indexed by a block table. That cuts memory waste from 60-80% down to under 4%, letting servers batch far more requests at once.

slides.title: Your GPU Is Wasting Most of Its KV Cache
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates needs its key/value vectors kept around for attention. That KV cache is often the single biggest consumer of GPU memory during serving — bigger than the model weights for long conversations.
bullets: KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and batch size
Naive serving reserves memory upfront for the worst case

slides.title: Contiguous Allocation Fragments Badly
slides.body: Early serving systems allocated one contiguous slab of GPU memory per request, sized for the maximum possible sequence length (e.g. 2048 tokens) — even if the request only generates 20 tokens before stopping.
bullets: Internal fragmentation: unused slots inside a reserved-but-unfilled slab
External fragmentation: free memory chopped into gaps too small to reuse
Published measurements found 60-80% of reserved KV cache memory went completely unused
Wasted memory directly caps how many requests you can batch together

slides.title: Page the KV Cache Like an OS Pages RAM
slides.body: PagedAttention splits each sequence's KV cache into fixed-size blocks (commonly 16 tokens each) that don't need to sit next to each other in memory. A per-sequence block table maps logical token positions to physical block addresses — exactly how a page table maps virtual to physical memory.
bullets: Blocks are allocated on demand, one at a time, as generation proceeds
No upfront reservation for a worst-case sequence length
The attention kernel reads the block table to gather scattered blocks at compute time
Reported overhead from the extra indirection: roughly 20-26% kernel latency, far outweighed by batching gains

slides.title: Copy-on-Write Lets Sequences Share Blocks
slides.body: Because blocks are reference-counted, requests that share a prefix — the same system prompt, or parallel samples from one input — can point at the same physical blocks instead of duplicating them.
bullets: Beam search: candidate beams share the common prefix's blocks
Parallel sampling (n>1 completions): one prompt's blocks are shared across all samples
A block is only copied when a sequence actually writes a divergent token into it
This is the same copy-on-write idea Unix uses for fork()

slides.title: The Throughput Payoff
slides.body: Near-zero fragmentation means far more requests fit in the same GPU memory at once, which is what actually drives serving throughput.
bullets: Gains are largest for workloads with highly variable output lengths
Gains shrink when every request already generates close to the max length

slides.title: Worked Example: A Shared System Prompt
slides.body: Say 8 customer-support requests all start with the same 500-token system prompt, then diverge into different questions.
bullets: Without paging: 8 separate copies of the 500-token prefix's KV cache are materialized
With PagedAttention: all 8 sequences' block tables point at the SAME physical blocks for those first ~31 blocks (16 tokens each)
Only the blocks covering each sequence's unique question get copied/allocated
Net effect: memory cost for the shared prefix drops roughly 8x in this scenario

slides.title: When It Matters — and When It Doesn't
slides.body: PagedAttention is now the default memory manager in vLLM and has influenced most production LLM serving stacks (TensorRT-LLM, SGLang, and others ship conceptually similar paging).
bullets: Biggest win: high-throughput multi-tenant serving with variable-length outputs
Smaller win: single-request, fixed-length batch jobs where fragmentation was never the bottleneck
Pitfall: the block-table indirection adds a small per-kernel latency tax — don't adopt it purely for single-request latency
Pairs naturally with continuous batching, which also needs fine-grained memory to admit new requests mid-batch

questions.prompt: What is the primary problem PagedAttention solves?
options: Slow attention matrix multiplication on GPUs
Memory fragmentation and waste from reserving contiguous KV cache slabs upfront
Inaccurate attention scores for long sequences
Slow tokenization of input prompts
questions.explanation: Naive serving reserved a contiguous block sized for the worst-case sequence length per request, wasting 60-80% of allocated KV cache memory to internal/external fragmentation. PagedAttention allocates small fixed-size blocks on demand instead.

questions.prompt: How does PagedAttention let parallel samples of the same prompt save memory?
options: It compresses the KV cache with quantization
It discards the KV cache for finished samples immediately
It uses copy-on-write so sequences share physical blocks for identical prefixes until they diverge
It recomputes the prefix's attention from scratch for each sample
questions.explanation: Reference-counted blocks let multiple sequences point at the same physical memory for a shared prefix. A block is only copied once a sequence writes a token that diverges from the others — the same copy-on-write pattern used by fork() in Unix.

questions.prompt: When does PagedAttention provide the LEAST benefit?
options: Multi-tenant serving with wildly different output lengths per request
Beam search with many shared candidate prefixes
A single request type that always generates exactly the maximum sequence length
Serving many requests that share a long system prompt
questions.explanation: If every request already fills its reserved slab (no variance in output length), there's little fragmentation to eliminate in the first place — the technique's gains come precisely from variable-length workloads and prefix sharing.

posts.title: CodeMender: An AI Agent That Patches Your PRs
posts.subtitle: Google wires its autonomous vulnerability-fixing agent straight into the pull request loop, with sandboxed exploits and keyless auth.
posts.summary: On November 11, 2026, Google Cloud published a reference architecture that runs CodeMender, its autonomous code-security agent, directly inside GitHub pull requests via Cloud Run. Scans, exploit verification, and patch generation now happen as slash commands in the PR thread, with exploit code sandboxed in network-isolated microVMs and no stored API keys.

slides.title: An AI Agent Just Joined Your Pull Request Queue
slides.body: Google Cloud shipped a reference architecture that runs its autonomous security agent, CodeMender, as a participant in the PR thread itself — not as a report you read after the fact.

slides.title: Code Ships Faster Than Flaws Get Fixed
slides.body: Agentic coding tools widened a gap that was already growing.
bullets: DORA data cited in the post: AI-assisted teams are shipping code at up to 2x their prior velocity
Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 Report: average time to fix a known software flaw grew from ~59 days a decade ago to more than 170 days in 2025
Most security review still happens after merge, as a separate queue competing for the same engineers who just shipped the code

slides.title: Scan, Verify, Fix, Approve — All as PR Comments
slides.body: The workflow lives entirely inside the pull request timeline, run on Cloud Run.
bullets: A PR triggers a scan; the bot posts one comment with a table of findings, each tagged with an ID
/verify <id> replies with the exploit attempt and a response trace, in a collapsible block
/fix <id> opens a draft PR with the patch behind a 'Preview Proposed Code Diff' section
/approve commits the patch, pushes it, and flips the commit status security/codemender-gate to green

slides.title: Three CLI Verbs Do the Real Work
slides.body: Under the slash commands sits a small, composable CLI.
bullets: cm find — analyzes code, returns a confidence score per finding
cm verify — if confidence is below 100%, builds and simulates an exploit in a sandbox; can change a finding's severity
cm fix <hash> — authors a patch for a finding that's already been verified
Verification artifacts stream to Cloud Storage, since the sandbox itself is ephemeral — that's the audit trail for compliance review

slides.title: Example: A Deserialization Bug Gets Caught Mid-PR
slides.body: A concrete pass through the loop.
bullets: A PR adds a new endpoint that deserializes user-supplied data; the Cloud Run scan flags it as finding a1b2c3d4
A reviewer comments /verify a1b2c3d4 — CodeMender builds the exploit in an isolated sandbox and posts the trace showing it actually fires
The reviewer comments /fix a1b2c3d4 — a draft PR opens with the patch diff for review
After reading the diff, the reviewer comments /approve — the patch is pushed and the security/codemender-gate status turns green

slides.title: Before vs. After the Integration

rows: Inside the PR thread, before merge
Manual reproduction, if anyone has time
cm verify builds and runs the exploit in a sandbox
cm fix drafts it as an open PR for review
security/codemender-gate status, enforced only if branch protection requires it

slides.title: The Gate Is Advisory Until You Turn On Branch Protection
slides.body: The post is explicit about three sharp edges.
bullets: Without a branch protection rule requiring the status check, security/codemender-gate is just a label — nothing stops the merge
Fail-open risk: a verification harness that only looks for a 'success' string can mislabel a sandbox crash or timeout as 'safe' instead of inconclusive
Exploit code is unreviewed and AI-generated, so it runs in a 2nd-gen Cloud Run microVM with no registry access, no outbound network route, and a minimal service account — 'only the verdict leaves'
The OIDC trust (Workload Identity Federation) must bind to immutable repository_id, not the repository name — names can be renamed or reclaimed by someone else

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: CodeMender now runs as slash commands inside the PR thread: scan, /verify, /fix, /approve
The real safety boundary is infrastructure, not the agent: ephemeral sandboxes, no stored keys, no outbound network from the exploit runner
A green security/codemender-gate status only blocks a merge if branch protection is configured to require it
Treat 'inconclusive' and 'safe' as different verdicts — a crashed or timed-out verification run proves nothing

questions.prompt: What actually makes CodeMender's green commit status block a bad merge?
options: The agent automatically closes the PR if it finds anything
A branch protection rule configured to require that status check
GitHub blocks any PR with open security comments by default
Nothing — CodeMender only advises, it can't gate merges
questions.explanation: The post is explicit: without a branch protection rule requiring the security/codemender-gate check, the status is advisory only — it shows up, but nothing stops the merge.

questions.prompt: Why does the Workload Identity Federation setup match on GitHub's repository_id instead of the repository name?
options: repository_id is shorter and faster to compare
Repository names are case-sensitive and IDs aren't
Names can be renamed or reclaimed by someone else, but the numeric ID is immutable
GitHub doesn't expose repository names in OIDC tokens
questions.explanation: Every GitHub Actions workflow shares the same OIDC issuer, so the attribute_condition does the real access-control work. Matching on a mutable field like the repo name risks a renamed or reclaimed repository inheriting trust it shouldn't have.

questions.prompt: Why should a crashed or timed-out exploit verification run be marked 'inconclusive' rather than 'safe'?
options: Because inconclusive results are cheaper to store in Cloud Storage
Because a crash always means the vulnerability doesn't exist
Because marking it 'safe' by default creates a fail-open gap — a crash isn't proof of safety
Because GitHub requires a third status category by policy
questions.explanation: The post warns about fail-open behavior directly: if a harness only searches for a successful exploit string, a crash or timeout can wrongly look like 'no exploit found,' when really the test just didn't run to completion.

posts.title: MCP Sampling: Letting Servers Borrow Your LLM
posts.subtitle: One request type lets an MCP server use the client's model mid-task — without ever holding an API key of its own.
posts.summary: MCP's sampling/createMessage request flips the protocol's usual direction: instead of a client calling a server's tool, a server asks the client to run a completion on its behalf. The client reviews the prompt, picks the model, reviews the output, and only then hands the result back — so the server gets real LLM reasoning without ever owning a model key.

slides.title: The Server That Has No Model of Its Own
slides.body: Most MCP servers are plumbing: query a database, call an API, return rows. Sampling is for the moment a server genuinely needs a model's judgment mid-task — and would rather borrow one than own one.

slides.title: Why Give Every Server Its Own API Key?
slides.body: Before sampling, a server that wanted LLM reasoning had only one option.
bullets: Ship its own provider API key, pick its own model, and eat its own bill — for every server author, independently
Lock the server's 'intelligence' to whichever model its author chose, not the one the user actually trusts and is paying for
Scatter credentials across every MCP server a user connects, instead of keeping model access in one place: the client

slides.title: sampling/createMessage: the Server Asks, the Client Decides
slides.body: The direction is reversed from a normal tool call.
bullets: The server sends a sampling/createMessage request up to the client — not the other way around
The client reviews the request, can edit the proposed prompt, and is the one that actually calls an LLM
The client reviews the completion before it ever reaches the server
The server never sees a model name, an API key, or a bill — it just gets back a finished message

slides.title: modelPreferences, Not a Model Name
slides.body: A server can't just demand a specific model.
bullets: A server can't request 'claude-opus-5' by name — the client might not have access to it, or might route to a different provider entirely
Instead it sends normalized 0–1 priorities for cost, speed, and intelligence, plus optional soft model-family hints
Hints are advisory: the client can map a hint to an equivalent model from an entirely different provider, or ignore it
Multiple hints are considered in order of preference — they're a suggestion, never a command

slides.title: Example: Summarizing 40 Tickets Without a Server-Side Model
slides.body: A ticket-tracker MCP server needs to turn a pile of raw data into one useful answer.
bullets: A tool call fetches 40 tickets related to a recurring bug — too much raw text to return usefully
Instead of dumping it all, the server issues sampling/createMessage asking for a root-cause summary drafted from the 40 tickets
The client's UI can show the user the draft prompt before it's sent, and let them edit or deny it outright
Once approved, the completion comes back to the server, which returns only the short summary as its tool result

slides.title: Normal Tool Call vs. Sampling Request

rows: Neither — the server borrows the client's model
Reviewing/editing both the prompt and the completion
Summarize, judge, or draft text inside a tool

slides.title: Sampling Is Opt-In, Slower, and Not Guaranteed
slides.body: Three limits worth designing around.
bullets: A client isn't required to support sampling at all — servers must handle a client that simply can't or won't run it
Every round-trip adds a human-in-the-loop pause (or at least a client-side LLM call) inside what looked like one tool call — a bad fit for latency-sensitive paths
Model hints are advisory only — a server tuned against one model family can get back a very different model from the client's chosen provider
Don't reach for sampling to dodge a good tool design — if the server can just compute the answer directly, a plain tool call beats an extra LLM hop

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Sampling flips MCP's usual direction: the server asks, the client supplies the model
It lets a server use real LLM reasoning without ever holding a provider API key or choosing a model
modelPreferences hints at cost/speed/intelligence tradeoffs, but the client always has final say on the actual model
Human review of both the prompt and the completion is the whole safety model here — treat it as load-bearing, not optional UI

questions.prompt: When an MCP server needs a completion, which direction does the sampling/createMessage request travel?
options: From the client to the server
From the server to the client
Directly from the server to an LLM provider's API
From one MCP server to a peer MCP server
questions.explanation: Sampling reverses MCP's usual flow. Instead of a client invoking a server's tool, the server sends sampling/createMessage up to the client, which is the one that actually talks to an LLM.

questions.prompt: Why can't a server just ask for a specific model like 'claude-opus-5' by name in a sampling request?
options: Model names aren't valid JSON strings
The client may not have access to that exact model, or may prefer a different provider's equivalent — so servers send priority hints instead
Only the first server to connect is allowed to pick a model
Sampling requests are not allowed to mention any model information at all
questions.explanation: Servers send modelPreferences as normalized cost/speed/intelligence priorities plus soft hints, not a hard model name — the client makes the final call on which model actually runs.

questions.prompt: What should a server assume about client support for sampling?
options: Every MCP client is required to support it
A client may not support sampling at all, so the server must handle that case
Only Claude-based clients can ever support it
Sampling requests always complete in under 100ms since no API key is involved
questions.explanation: Sampling support is not guaranteed across every client. A well-built server has a fallback path for when the client can't or won't run a sampling request.

posts.title: Claude Can Now Open and Edit Your Actual Apps
posts.subtitle: Interactive connectors grow from tiny previews into full apps running beside the chat.
posts.summary: On November 10, 2026, Anthropic let partner apps open as full, side-by-side or full-screen tools inside Claude, with Claude editing directly in your signed-in account under your approval. It runs on MCP Apps, an open protocol extension, so these apps aren't locked to Claude.

slides.title: Connectors Used to Mean Tiny Previews
slides.body: Interactive connectors launched earlier in 2026 let a connected tool show a small live view inside the conversation — useful for a glance, useless for real work.
bullets: A live view ≠ the real app — no full editor, no your-account access
Any actual edit meant tabbing away to the tool itself and back
Claude could describe changes, but you verified them somewhere else

slides.title: Full Apps Now Open Beside — or Instead of — the Chat

slides.title: Under the Hood: MCP Apps

bullets: MCP Apps lets an MCP server ship its own interface, not just text responses
Any AI application that supports the extension can run the same app — Claude just supports more of it now (app tools + embedded sites)
Developer-side MCP Apps support is still in public preview

You review the changes and approve the edit before anything saves — same approval flow as any connector action

Coverage is still partial: check whether your specific connector has been upgraded before relying on it

posts.title: CRDTs: Merging Edits Without a Referee
posts.subtitle: How two people can edit the same document offline and still end up in sync.
posts.summary: A CRDT (Conflict-free Replicated Data Type) is a data structure whose merge rule is mathematically guaranteed to converge, no matter what order updates arrive in. That lets apps support real-time, even offline, multi-user editing without a central server deciding who's right.

slides.title: Two People, One Document, Zero Conflicts
slides.body: CRDTs make 'merge conflict' disappear by designing the data structure so there's nothing left to argue about.

slides.title: The Old Options Both Have a Cost
slides.body: Before CRDTs, collaborative systems picked between two unpleasant tradeoffs.
bullets: Pessimistic locking: only one editor at a time — everyone else waits on a mutex
Naive last-write-wins: the second save silently overwrites the first editor's work
Both need a reachable central coordinator — exactly what you don't have on a flaky connection or offline

slides.title: The Trick: a Merge Function That Can't Disagree
slides.body: A CRDT's merge operation is commutative, associative, and idempotent — so applying the same set of updates in any order, any number of times, lands every replica in the identical final state.
bullets: Commutative: merge(A, B) = merge(B, A) — order of arrival doesn't matter
Associative: merging in any grouping gives the same result
Idempotent: merging the same update twice changes nothing
No coordinator needed — any two replicas can merge directly, even peer-to-peer, even offline

slides.title: The Building Blocks
slides.body: CRDTs aren't one data structure — they're a family, each solving a different conflict shape.
bullets: G-Counter: grow-only counter; each replica tracks its own increments, merge = take the max seen per replica, then sum
PN-Counter: a G-Counter for increments plus one for decrements, so values can go down too
LWW-Register: last-write-wins on a single value, tie-broken by timestamp + replica ID
OR-Set: tags every add with a unique ID, so a concurrent add and remove resolve deterministically instead of racing
Sequence CRDTs (e.g. RGA): give every inserted character a stable position anchored to its neighbor — this is what lets real-time text editors interleave concurrent typing correctly

slides.title: Example: Two Phones, One Note, No Signal
slides.body: Two people edit the same shared note on a flight, both offline.
bullets: Person A inserts a word at the start of paragraph 2; Person B inserts a different word at the end of the same paragraph
Each inserted character carries a unique ID anchored to the character before it — not a numeric index
On landing, both devices exchange their update logs and merge
Because positions are relative, not index-based, both insertions land correctly with no index collisions — no server ever had to decide an order

slides.title: CRDT vs. Operational Transformation

rows: Transforms each op against every concurrent op it crossed in flight
Usually yes — a server sequences operations
Merge function is mathematically guaranteed to converge regardless of arrival order
No — replicas can merge directly, even offline

slides.title: Where CRDTs Fall Short
slides.body: Convergence isn't free, and it isn't a cure-all.
bullets: Tombstones: many CRDTs must remember deleted elements (not truly erase them) to stay commutative — metadata grows unless you garbage-collect it
Structural convergence ≠ business correctness: merging two concurrent '-$50' withdrawals on a balance converges mathematically, but may not be what the business wants
Not everything marketed as 'real-time collaboration' is a true CRDT — some well-known multiplayer engines are CRDT-inspired but still rely on a central server to order events
Best fit: free-form content like text, drawings, and counters — worse fit for data with hard invariants like account balances

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: A CRDT is defined by its merge function: commutative, associative, idempotent → guaranteed convergence
Different CRDT types (counters, registers, sets, sequences) solve different conflict shapes
They enable offline-first, peer-to-peer collaboration that locking and last-write-wins can't
They trade metadata growth and 'structural-only' correctness for that guarantee — pick the right tool for data with hard business invariants

questions.prompt: What three properties must a CRDT's merge function have to guarantee every replica converges to the same state?
options: Fast, cheap, and simple
Commutative, associative, and idempotent
Encrypted, signed, and timestamped
Synchronous, atomic, and serializable
questions.explanation: Commutative (order doesn't matter), associative (grouping doesn't matter), and idempotent (repeating doesn't matter) together guarantee that any set of replicas applying the same updates in any order end up identical — no coordinator required.

questions.prompt: Which CRDT type is specifically designed so a concurrent 'add' and 'remove' of the same set element resolve without ambiguity?
options: G-Counter
LWW-Register
OR-Set
PN-Counter
questions.explanation: An OR-Set (Observed-Remove Set) tags every add with a unique identifier. A remove only removes the specific adds it has actually observed, so a concurrent add can survive a stale, in-flight remove instead of racing it.

questions.prompt: What's a genuine limitation of CRDTs compared to a centralized lock?
options: They cannot work when devices are offline
Tombstones and per-element metadata can grow unbounded without periodic cleanup
They require every client to run the same programming language
They cannot represent ordered text at all
questions.explanation: To stay commutative, many CRDTs keep tombstones for deleted elements instead of truly erasing them. Without periodic garbage collection, that bookkeeping metadata keeps growing — a real operational cost locking doesn't have.

posts.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: The Cheapest Model Anthropic Has Shipped
posts.subtitle: 90% cheaper, tunable effort, and fast enough to be everyone else's sidekick
posts.summary: Anthropic shipped Claude Haiku 5.5 as its cheapest, fastest small model yet, with a first-ever adjustable effort dial and up to 90% lower cost than Haiku 4.5 — built to run the high-volume grunt work behind agents powered by Opus or Sonnet.

slides.title: Anthropic's cheapest, fastest model yet
slides.body: Released October 7, 2026: Claude Haiku 5.5 targets the unglamorous majority of LLM calls — summaries, classification, database lookups, context compaction — the volume work that makes agent systems expensive.

slides.title: Big models are overkill for most LLM calls
slides.body: A production agent doesn't spend most of its tokens reasoning — it spends them summarizing, classifying, and compacting context. Running that volume through a frontier model burns budget for no quality gain.
bullets: High-volume tasks: summaries, compactions, database queries, classification
Sonnet 5.5 input costs $2.00/1M tokens vs. Haiku 4.5's $1.00/1M — and both are overkill for a one-line classification call
Multi-agent systems need a cheap subagent that Opus/Sonnet can delegate grunt work to

slides.title: A dial for effort, not just a smaller model
slides.body: Haiku 5.5 is the first Haiku-class model with an adjustable effort setting — Low, Med, High, Xhigh, Max — letting one model trade latency for quality per call instead of switching models.
bullets: Effort levels: Low / Med / High / Xhigh / Max — tune per request
Designed to run as a subagent alongside Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 during coding workflows
Updated tokenizer means it uses slightly more tokens per task than Haiku 4.5 — a real tradeoff, not pure upside

slides.title: The price drop is the headline, not the benchmarks
slides.body: Haiku 5.5 beats Haiku 4.5 on every public benchmark Anthropic published, and even edges past GPT-6 Luna on most of them — but it still trails Sonnet 5.5 by a wide margin on hard agentic work.

slides.title: What early customers actually measured
slides.body: Anthropic's launch post cites concrete, named deployments rather than synthetic benchmarks — the kind of evidence that matters more than a leaderboard score.
bullets: Asana: over 30% lower latency per task, up to 2.5x faster inference per agent turn
AlphaSense: 0.84 relevance score vs. 0.76 for Haiku 4.5 across 400 real queries
Box: scored 11 points higher than Haiku 4.5 at roughly half the latency
Cognition's Devin Fusion hit a FrontierCode score of 66.2 using Haiku 5.5 as the sidekick model

slides.title: Where Haiku 5.5 is the wrong tool
slides.body: Cheap and fast isn't free of tradeoffs. The same benchmark table that flatters Haiku 5.5 against its predecessor still shows a 30+ point gap against Sonnet 5.5 on genuinely hard agentic work.
bullets: Terminal-Bench 4.0: 39.2% (Haiku 5.5) vs. 70.6% (Sonnet 5.5) — don't hand it complex multi-step coding
Cybersecurity safeguards are more restrictive than Haiku 4.5's and still block penetration-testing use cases
The new tokenizer uses more tokens per task, eating into some of the per-token price win on short prompts

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Haiku 5.5 isn't trying to out-reason Opus or Sonnet — it's trying to make the 80% of agent calls that don't need a frontier model almost free.
bullets: Up to 90% cheaper than Haiku 4.5 for prompts under 100k tokens, per Anthropic's own footnote
First Haiku model with a tunable effort dial (Low → Max) instead of a fixed capability tier
Built to be the cheap subagent under Opus/Sonnet-led coding workflows, not a standalone replacement for them

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Search Skips Most of the Haystack
posts.subtitle: The graph structure that makes billion-vector search feel instant
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based index that powers approximate nearest-neighbor search in almost every modern vector database. By organizing vectors into layered graphs and searching greedily from sparse to dense, it turns a search that should cost millions of comparisons into one that costs a few dozen.

slides.title: Finding your nearest neighbor without checking everyone
slides.body: Every RAG pipeline, recommendation engine, and semantic search box eventually asks the same question: which stored vectors are closest to this query vector? HNSW is how that question gets answered in milliseconds at scale.

slides.title: Brute-force search doesn't scale past a toy dataset
slides.body: Exact nearest-neighbor search means comparing the query embedding against every stored vector — O(N) distance computations per query.
bullets: 10K vectors: brute force is fine, sub-millisecond
10M vectors: every query now does 10 million distance computations
A RAG app serving concurrent users can't afford a full linear scan on every retrieval call
Exact search also doesn't get faster as you add more dimensions — high-dimensional embeddings make the 'curse of dimensionality' worse, not better

slides.title: Layered graphs, like a highway system
slides.body: HNSW builds multiple stacked graph layers. The top layer is sparse with long-range connections (highways); the bottom layer is dense with short-range connections (local streets). Every node lives in the bottom layer, but only some nodes exist in higher layers.
bullets: Each node is a stored vector; edges connect it to its approximate nearest neighbors
Node → max layer is chosen randomly at insert time (fewer nodes reach higher layers, by design)
Parameter M caps how many neighbor edges each node keeps per layer — typically 12-48
More layers = fewer 'hops' needed to cross the whole dataset, same idea as a skip list

slides.title: Search: start sparse, zoom in, land dense
slides.body: A query starts at a fixed entry point in the top layer and greedily walks to whichever neighbor is closest to the query — then drops down a layer and repeats, narrowing in like a zoom lens.
bullets: Top layer: a handful of greedy hops gets you roughly to the right neighborhood
Each lower layer refines the position with denser local connections
ef (search-time candidate list size) controls how many candidates are tracked — higher ef = better recall, slower query
efConstruction controls the same tradeoff at build time — how carefully each node's neighbors are chosen when the index is created

slides.title: HNSW vs. the alternatives
slides.body: No index is free — HNSW trades memory and build complexity for query speed and strong recall, which is why it's the default in most vector databases but not the only option.

slides.title: Worked example: searching 10M product embeddings
slides.body: A shopping app embeds 10 million product descriptions. A user searches "wireless earbuds under $50." The query gets embedded, then HNSW is asked for the top 20 nearest product vectors.
bullets: Brute force: ~10M cosine-similarity comparisons — too slow for a live request at any real concurrency
HNSW: the query enters at the top layer's entry point, takes a few greedy hops toward the "electronics/audio" neighborhood, then descends through denser layers to pinpoint the 20 closest listings
Total comparisons end up in the dozens-to-low-hundreds range instead of millions, because most of the graph is never visited
The catalog can be re-ranked afterward (e.g., by price, in-stock status) — HNSW's job is just getting a fast, high-recall shortlist

slides.title: When HNSW is the wrong call
slides.body: HNSW is approximate by design, and that approximation has real costs beyond raw speed.
bullets: It's approximate — you can miss the true nearest neighbor; if you need exact results on a small dataset, brute force is simpler and sufficient
Graph edges cost real memory — expect noticeably more RAM than the raw vectors alone, which matters at hundreds of millions of vectors
Deleting vectors is awkward: removing a node can fragment its neighbors' connections, so most implementations tombstone-and-rebuild rather than delete cleanly
Index build time grows with efConstruction and dataset size — a very high-recall index isn't free to construct, either

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: HNSW is the reason "semantic search over millions of documents" feels instant instead of batch-job slow — it's the default ANN index in FAISS, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, and pgvector for exactly this reason.
bullets: Trades exactness for speed: a layered graph lets search skip most of the dataset instead of scanning it
Tune ef / efConstruction to trade recall against latency for your workload — there's no universal best setting
Expect a real memory premium over raw vector storage; budget for it before you pick HNSW at scale
Favor IVF or a managed index if you need frequent deletes or tight memory, not just raw query speed

questions.prompt: Why does HNSW use multiple stacked graph layers instead of one flat graph?
options: To store multiple copies of each vector for redundancy
So that the top sparse layers let search take big jumps toward the right neighborhood before lower, denser layers refine the exact result
Because GPUs require data split into layers
To allow different embedding models to share the same index
questions.explanation: The layering is the core trick: sparse top layers act like highways for long jumps, and denser bottom layers narrow in on the precise nearest neighbors — similar to how a skip list speeds up search.

questions.prompt: What does increasing the `ef` parameter at search time do?
options: It deletes stale vectors from the index
It increases recall by tracking more candidates, at the cost of slower queries
It changes the embedding model being used
It has no effect on HNSW search
questions.explanation: `ef` controls the size of the dynamic candidate list during search. A larger value explores more of the graph, improving the odds of finding the true nearest neighbors, but it costs more time per query.

questions.prompt: Which limitation is most specific to HNSW, compared to a simple brute-force index?
options: It cannot be used with cosine similarity
It only works with text embeddings, not images
It can miss the true nearest neighbor because it searches approximately, and deletions are awkward because they fragment graph connections
It requires a GPU to run at all
questions.explanation: HNSW's speed comes from approximation — it doesn't guarantee the exact nearest neighbor — and because results depend on graph connectivity, removing nodes cleanly is harder than in a flat list, which is why many systems tombstone instead of truly deleting.

posts.title: StudentSim: Training AI to Simulate Real Students
posts.subtitle: Microsoft Research builds personalized student models so AI tutors can be trained and tested without a live classroom.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research's StudentSim trains personalized LLM simulators of real students so AI tutors can be evaluated and trained without needing live learners. On chess coaching, a tutor reinforcement-learned against StudentSim's feedback reached 90.5% expert-rated accuracy, beating both a no-RL baseline (75.7%) and a generic-LLM-reward baseline (71.6%).

slides.title: A fake student that actually acts like your real one
bullets: Testing AI tutors usually means running studies with real learners — slow, expensive, and hard to iterate on quickly.
StudentSim builds a per-student LLM simulator that predicts both a student's answers and how those answers change after coaching.

slides.title: Role-playing an LLM as 'a student' doesn't work
bullets: A generic LLM told to 'act like a struggling student' is usually far more capable than the real learner it's supposed to stand in for.
That lets a tutor look effective against an opponent it could never actually help in real life.
Education research says a good proxy needs two separate properties: it must match the student's real ability (fidelity), and it must change its answers realistically after guidance (responsiveness).

slides.title: Two-stage training turns logs into a personal simulator
bullets: Stage 1: train on records pooled across many students in a domain (chess, ESL writing, math) to learn common error and revision patterns.
Stage 2: specialize that base model on one student's de-identified history to capture their personal ability level.
StudentSimEval then scores every simulator on both axes: fidelity (does it match held-out real answers?) and guidance responsiveness (does it update after reading tutor feedback?).

slides.title: The numbers: StudentSim beats both baselines at once
bullets: Maia2, a dedicated chess-move predictor, matches real moves reasonably well but barely updates after coaching — it models playing style, not learning.
A prompted GPT-5.4 'play like a student' baseline updates too eagerly but tracks the real student's actual choices far less closely.
StudentSim wins on both axes simultaneously — a useful student proxy has to be realistic AND teachable.

slides.title: Using the simulator to train a better chess tutor
bullets: A frozen StudentSim reads a tutor's advice and predicts the move the real student would play after hearing it.
The reward signal is the improvement in that resulting move's quality, scored by the Stockfish chess engine.
The tutor is then reinforcement-learned directly against this reward, instead of against a generic LLM's guess or no RL at all.

slides.title: Training against StudentSim produced a measurably better tutor
bullets: Rewarding the tutor with a generic LLM's guess at 'did this help' made it worse than no RL at all — it optimized for the wrong signal.
Rewarding it with StudentSim's prediction of the real student's revised move pushed blind expert-rated accuracy to 90.5%, with higher ratings for personalization too.

slides.title: Where this breaks down
bullets: StudentSim is a research signal, not a replacement for real-learner studies — it hasn't been tested in live classrooms.
It's trained and evaluated only on public, de-identified datasets in three narrow domains: chess, ESL essays, and multiple-choice math.
A simulator this personalized needs real per-student interaction logs to specialize — it can't model a new student from zero history.

slides.title: What to remember
bullets: Optimizing an AI tutor against the wrong proxy (a too-capable LLM) can make it measurably worse, not just unhelpfully neutral.
Good simulators need two scores, not one: match real behavior (fidelity) and react correctly to intervention (responsiveness).
This is a template, not just a chess result — the same two-stage recipe is applied to ESL writing and math coaching in the same work.

questions.prompt: Why did rewarding a chess tutor with a generic 'play like a student' LLM make it perform worse (71.6%) than no reinforcement learning at all (75.7%)?
options: Because the generic LLM reward signal didn't track how the real student would actually respond, so the tutor optimized for the wrong target
Because reinforcement learning always degrades tutor performance
Because GPT-5.4 is a weaker model than Maia2
Because Stockfish gave inconsistent move-quality scores
questions.explanation: The reward has to reflect what actually helps the real student. A too-capable generic 'student' lets the tutor get credit for guidance a real learner wouldn't actually use correctly — so training against it pushes the tutor in the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between 'behavioral fidelity' and 'guidance responsiveness' in StudentSimEval?
options: Fidelity measures how closely the simulator matches real recorded answers; responsiveness measures whether it updates correctly after reading tutor guidance
They measure the same thing using different chess engines
Fidelity is for math domains only, responsiveness is for chess only
Responsiveness measures how fast the model generates text
questions.explanation: A simulator needs both: look like the real student on held-out problems (fidelity), and actually change its answer in a realistic way after coaching (responsiveness). Maia2 shows you can have one without the other.

questions.prompt: Maia2, a chess engine tuned to predict human moves, scored well on fidelity (0.454) but poorly on responsiveness (0.272). What does that reveal?
options: Predicting what a student currently plays is a different skill from predicting how that student learns from feedback
Maia2 is simply a worse model than GPT-5.4 at everything
Chess is too complex a domain to simulate at all
Responsiveness scores are always lower than fidelity scores by design
questions.explanation: Maia2 was built to mimic current playing style, not to model learning. It's a reminder that matching behavior and modeling change-after-guidance are genuinely separate capabilities a simulator needs both of.

posts.title: Quine: Microsoft's AI World Model for Biology
posts.subtitle: A multimodal model that predicts how biological systems respond to interventions, built with the Broad Institute.
posts.summary: Microsoft Research and the Broad Institute introduced Quine, a multimodal 'world model' of biology paired with a scientist-in-the-loop harness. In a pancreatic cancer case study, it correctly predicted which compounds would shift tumor cell states, which shifts would be weaker, and even flagged an unexpected third outcome — all confirmed in wet-lab validation.

slides.title: A model that predicts biology before the lab does
bullets: Microsoft Research, with the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, introduced Quine on September 29, 2026 — a research-only AI system for biology.
It pairs a multimodal 'world model' of biological systems with a harness connecting models, lab tools, literature, and scientists.

slides.title: Biology's bottleneck is search space, not just lab speed
bullets: Wet-lab experiments are slow and expensive, but the deeper problem is combinatorial: far too many possible interventions to test by trial and error.
Existing specialist models typically handle one data type at a time — genomics, or protein structure, or imaging — so evidence from one modality can't directly sharpen predictions in another.

slides.title: One shared representation across five kinds of biological data
bullets: Quine's world model learns joint representations across sequence, protein structure, chemistry, RNA/cellular state, and bioimaging — instead of running separate models per data type.
Because the representation is shared, evidence collected in one modality (say, imaging) can sharpen predictions made in another (say, which compound to test next).
A harness layer orchestrates reasoning models on top of the world model and connects them to scientific tools, published literature, and the researchers running the loop.

slides.title: The loop: predict, test, refine
bullets: Scientists pose a question; Quine proposes candidates in silico; a wet lab tests the top-ranked ones; results feed back to refine both the next question and the model itself.
The explicit goal is to prioritize which experiments are worth running — not to replace experimentation.

slides.title: Case study: redirecting a pancreatic cancer cell state
bullets: Quine predicted and ranked thousands of compounds for their potential to shift pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells from one state to another.
A handful of its top-ranked candidates were validated in wet-lab assays; the highest-ranked compounds produced the largest intended shifts.
Some of the strongest hits worked through unexpected mechanisms — a signal the authors flag as a possible drug-repurposing lead.
Quine also predicted the reverse shift would be weaker, and predicted cells could move toward a third, different phenotype — both calls the lab experiments confirmed.

slides.title: What Quine is not — and why that matters
bullets: No formal quantitative benchmark is published; the public evidence so far is one detailed case study, not a leaderboard result.
Initial access is limited to the Quine Fellows program and select research collaborations — it isn't a public API or product yet.
Microsoft is explicit that outputs can be incomplete or wrong and need review by qualified researchers plus real experimental validation. It's for research, not clinical or medical use.

slides.title: What to remember
bullets: Quine's bet is that one shared world model across modalities beats a pipeline of narrow specialist models, because evidence transfers between data types.
The PDAC case study is convincing partly because Quine was right about an effect being weak, or going a third direction — not just right about the obvious call.
It's the same multimodal-world-model idea behind recent robotics and game-world models, pointed at wet-lab science instead.

questions.prompt: What makes Quine's 'world model' approach different from using separate specialist models for genomics, proteins, and imaging?
options: It learns a shared representation across data types, so evidence from one modality can inform predictions in another
It only works on one data type at a time, same as specialist models
It skips wet-lab validation entirely
It replaces the need for any biological data
questions.explanation: The core design choice is joint training across modalities instead of orchestrating separate per-modality models — that's what lets a signal in, say, imaging data sharpen a prediction about which compound to test.

questions.prompt: In the PDAC case study, what happened with the reverse (basal-to-classical) cell state shift?
options: Quine predicted it would be weaker than the forward shift, and the lab results matched that prediction
Quine predicted it would be the strongest effect, but the lab disproved this
The reverse shift was never tested
Quine refused to make a prediction about it
questions.explanation: A qualitatively weaker prediction that experiments then confirm is still a meaningful result — it shows the model's ranking captured a real asymmetry in the biology, not just noise.

questions.prompt: Why does Microsoft describe Quine as research-only with limited access rather than releasing it broadly?
options: Its outputs can be incomplete or inaccurate and need expert review plus wet-lab validation before they mean anything
It's too computationally expensive to run more than once a month
The Broad Institute requires every researcher to use it manually
It has already been proven unreliable in clinical trials
questions.explanation: The post is explicit that Quine prioritizes experiments to run, not final answers — treating a world model's predictions as settled fact without the validation loop is exactly the failure mode it's designed to avoid.

posts.title: Test-Time Compute: Making Models Think Longer, Not Bigger
posts.subtitle: Why spending more computation at inference time can beat training a bigger model from scratch.
posts.summary: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis, independent of model size: spend extra computation per query — longer reasoning chains, multiple sampled attempts, or search over reasoning paths — to trade inference cost for accuracy on a model that's already trained.

slides.title: Same model, more thinking, better answers
bullets: Test-time compute (also called inference-time scaling) means spending extra computation when the model answers a specific question — not when it's trained.
The clearest form is a reasoning model that generates a long chain of intermediate reasoning tokens before committing to a final answer.

slides.title: Training-time scaling was hitting diminishing returns
bullets: For years the default lever was 'bigger model, more training data' — but each additional order of magnitude of training compute buys smaller accuracy gains.
Many hard problems (multi-step math, competition coding, complex planning) aren't 'too big to know' — they're too easy to get wrong on the first attempt, regardless of model size.
That reframes the lever: instead of a model that knows more, build one that can check and revise its own work before answering.

slides.title: Three concrete ways to spend extra inference compute
bullets: Longer chains of thought: generate more reasoning tokens per answer before the final output — literally more forward passes before committing.
Best-of-N sampling: generate N candidate answers and pick the best one with a verifier, a scoring model, or majority vote (self-consistency).
Search over reasoning paths: branch into multiple partial solutions (tree-of-thought style search) and prune the weaker branches before continuing.

slides.title: Why this works: verification is often easier than generation
bullets: Checking whether a math proof step is valid, or whether code compiles and passes a test, is usually cheaper and more reliable than generating the correct step from scratch.
Test-time compute exploits that gap: generate many attempts relatively cheaply, then spend a little extra compute to verify and select.
It's the same intuition behind search-based game-playing systems: a weaker policy plus enough search at decision time can beat a stronger policy with no search.

slides.title: Matching the technique to the task
bullets: The more compute you spend per answer, the more you depend on having a way to tell a good answer from a bad one — plain majority voting is the weakest, free form of that check.

rows: Tasks with a cheap correctness check (code, math)
Hard combinatorial problems worth the cost

slides.title: A worked example: picking the right answer out of five
bullets: Ask a reasoning model a tricky probability question and sample 5 independent chains of thought instead of 1.
Self-consistency: if 4 of 5 chains land on the same final number, treat that as a much stronger signal than any single chain's confidence.
If a verifier is available — a unit test for a coding problem, say — you can skip the vote entirely: run all 5 candidate solutions and keep the one that actually passes.
This is strictly more expensive per question than asking once; it only pays off when getting it right matters more than getting it fast.

slides.title: When NOT to spend extra test-time compute
bullets: Simple, low-stakes queries ('what's the capital of France') gain nothing from extra reasoning tokens — it's pure latency and cost with no accuracy benefit.

Without a verifier, best-of-N on open-ended tasks (creative writing, subjective judgment calls) has no reliable way to pick the 'best' sample — majority vote doesn't even make sense when there's no single right answer.
Latency-sensitive products (autocomplete, real-time chat) often can't afford the extra seconds a long reasoning chain or N-way search adds, even if accuracy would improve.

slides.title: What to remember
bullets: Test-time compute is a second scaling axis independent of model size and training data — you can trade inference cost for accuracy on a fixed, already-trained model.
It works best exactly where verification is cheaper than generation: math, code, logic puzzles with checkable answers.

Match the technique to the task: longer chain-of-thought for reasoning depth, best-of-N plus a verifier when correctness is checkable, tree search when the problem is combinatorial enough to justify branching.

questions.prompt: Why does test-time compute often work especially well on math and coding problems?
options: Because checking whether an answer is correct (a proof step, a passing test) is usually cheaper and more reliable than generating the correct answer from scratch
Because math and coding problems have no correct answer, so any answer counts
Because reasoning models can only be applied to numerical data
Because longer chains of thought always reduce total token cost
questions.explanation: The core exploit is the gap between generation difficulty and verification difficulty. When verification is cheap and reliable, spending extra compute to generate-then-check pays off; when it isn't, that extra compute has nothing useful to select against.

questions.prompt: A team adds best-of-5 sampling with majority voting to a model answering open-ended creative writing prompts. What's the likely problem?
options: There's no single 'correct' answer to vote toward, so majority voting has no reliable signal to select the best sample
Creative writing prompts are too short for sampling to matter
Majority voting always picks the worst sample
Best-of-N sampling requires a GPU cluster to run at all
questions.explanation: Self-consistency and majority voting assume convergent correctness — many independent attempts should agree on one right answer. Open-ended, subjective tasks don't have that property, so the technique loses its justification.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between training-time scaling and test-time compute as levers for improving a model?
options: Training-time scaling grows the model and data before deployment; test-time compute spends extra computation per query on an already-trained model
They are two names for exactly the same technique
Test-time compute requires retraining the model from scratch for every question
Training-time scaling only applies to image models, not language models
questions.explanation: Training-time scaling is a one-time investment baked into the model's weights. Test-time compute is a per-query dial — you can turn it up for a hard question and down for an easy one, on the exact same trained model.

posts.title: AI-Guided Search Cracked a 31-Year-Old Math Conjecture
posts.subtitle: 100 candidate proof directions, pruned by humans, finished in a month.
posts.summary: Microsoft researchers resolved the 1995 KLS conjecture on high-dimensional convex geometry by pairing AI agents — which explored over 100 candidate proof strategies in parallel — with human mathematicians who pruned dead ends and assembled the final argument. Unguided AI models given the same token budget, without that human steering, failed to reach the result.

slides.title: A Problem Open Since 1995, Closed in October 2026
slides.body: Microsoft Research announced a full proof of the KLS conjecture, a central open question in high-dimensional convex geometry — reached through a structured, human-directed search where AI agents did the exploring.
bullets: Proposed in 1995 by Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits
Final proof completed October 4, 2026
Over 100 candidate approaches explored with AI assistance before the breakthrough

slides.title: What the KLS Conjecture Actually Asks
slides.body: For a high-dimensional convex body, cutting it in half with a flat hyperplane is easy to describe but not obviously optimal. The conjecture asks whether a flat cut is always nearly as good as the best cut of any shape — within a fixed constant, no matter how many dimensions you're in.
bullets: Example on a regular tetrahedron: the best flat cut has area 0.2500, the best curved cut about 0.2173 — close, but not equal
The conjecture says that gap never grows arbitrarily large as dimension increases
It matters because this cut geometry governs how fast random walks mix through a high-dimensional distribution — the engine behind most sampling algorithms

slides.title: Human-Directed AI Search, Not a Single Clever Insight
slides.body: The team didn't hand the problem to an AI model and wait. They ran a structured search: AI agents proposed and worked out candidate approaches — many involving long derivations with higher-order tensors — in parallel, in repeated rounds.
bullets: Over 100 candidate research directions explored before the breakthrough approach emerged
Each round: agents explore variations in parallel, a researcher reviews intermediate results, discards weak directions, and carries the best forward
AI tools handled derivations, manuscript drafting, and internal proof-checking; humans set the mathematical direction, picked which ideas to pursue, and assembled and verified the final argument
The key recursive-refinement idea — the thing that actually closed the proof — is credited to the human researchers, built on their earlier work on fast linear-programming algorithms

slides.title: Three Drafts, One Universal Constant
slides.body: The bound tightened in stages over a few months, each version posted to arXiv as the proof improved.

rows: Reduced to an iterated logarithm — still grows, just very slowly
Fixed universal constant — no dimension dependence at all

slides.title: When the Same AI Models Tried It Alone, They Fell Short
slides.body: In a separate track, the researchers let several leading AI models attempt the conjecture unguided — no human pruning dead ends between rounds — using roughly the same total token budget as the successful run.
bullets: The unguided attempts did not reach the result
The successful run's advantage wasn't more tokens — it was a human discarding unpromising directions after every round and redirecting the search
The researchers' own framing: success depended on both AI capability and human mathematical judgment, not either alone

slides.title: This Isn't "AI Solved Math" — Read the Fine Print
slides.body: The result is genuinely significant, but the framing matters for what it predicts about AI-assisted research elsewhere.
bullets: The proof still needed an expert to choose which of 100+ directions were worth pursuing — that judgment didn't come from the AI
Independent human verification mattered: two other groups posted their own full proofs the same day, one explicitly building on an early version of this paper
A Lean 4 formalization exists on GitHub, but the authors' own shortened, Lean-verified version isn't released yet — pending final review
The blog post doesn't name which AI models were used, so this isn't evidence for any one specific model's reasoning ability

slides.title: The Pattern: AI Widens the Search, Humans Narrow It
bullets: AI's contribution here was breadth — exploring 100+ directions in parallel that one person couldn't cover alone
Human contribution was depth of judgment — recognizing which partial results were worth building on, and supplying the original recursive-refinement idea
Unguided AI with the same compute budget did not reproduce the result — judgment wasn't optional
Expect this human-prune, AI-explore loop to show up in other hard, verifiable research domains before it shows up anywhere judgment can't be mechanically checked

questions.prompt: What does the KLS conjecture claim about cutting a high-dimensional convex body in half?
options: A flat (hyperplane) cut is always exactly optimal
The best flat cut is within a fixed universal constant of the best cut of any shape, regardless of dimension
Curved cuts are always better by a factor that grows with dimension
The conjecture is about sorting algorithms, not geometry
questions.explanation: The conjecture says the gap between the best flat cut and the best possible cut of any shape never grows unboundedly as dimensions increase — it's capped by a constant. This matters because that gap controls how fast random-walk sampling algorithms mix in high dimensions.

questions.prompt: How did the research team actually use AI to find the proof?
options: They gave one AI model the problem and let it run unsupervised until it finished
They ran a structured search: AI agents explored 100+ candidate directions in parallel rounds, with a human discarding weak ones and redirecting each round
AI wasn't involved at all — it was found by hand
They used AI only to typeset the final paper
questions.explanation: The breakthrough came from an iterative, human-pruned search: AI agents proposed and worked through many candidate approaches per round, and a researcher chose which to carry forward. That structure is what separated the successful run from unguided AI attempts.

questions.prompt: What happened when several leading AI models attempted the KLS conjecture unguided, with a similar total token budget to the successful run?
options: They solved it faster than the human-guided run
They fell short of the result
They proved a stronger, more general theorem
They refused to attempt the problem
questions.explanation: The unguided attempts, despite comparable compute, did not reach the proof. The researchers attribute the successful run's edge to human mathematical judgment steering the search — raw AI search volume alone wasn't sufficient.

Work can keep running for hours or days after you close your laptop

slides.title: The Problem: Siloed Bots, No Shared Memory
slides.body: Most enterprise AI deployments today are a patchwork — a chatbot in Slack, a separate coding assistant, a separate data-analysis tool — each with its own context that resets between sessions and no shared identity or audit trail.
bullets: Switching tools means re-explaining context every time
No consistent way to grant an agent least-privilege access to company systems, or audit what it did
No persistent execution: close the laptop, lose the in-progress work

slides.title: How It's Built: Orchestration, Four Memory Types, Model Choice
slides.body: The Gemini agent can spin up temporary, job-specific sub-agents, coordinate them in parallel or in sequence, and act as a persistent "coworker agent" with its own identity.
bullets: Coworker agents get their own storage and an address like name@agents.company.com
Four memory types: session, semantic, procedural (skills it writes for itself), and episodic
A routing layer sends each job to whichever model fits — Gemini or Anthropic's Claude models today, with other models planned
Connects to Confluence, Microsoft Office, Teams, Slack, Workspace, Git, Jira, Salesforce, ServiceNow, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, local files, and any MCP server

slides.title: Governance: Treating Agents Like Employees With Badges
slides.body: Because a coworker agent can act on company data unattended, Google built identity and spend controls around it rather than bolting them on later.
bullets: Each agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege, OAuth-propagated permissions
Agents run inside an "Agent Sandbox" with its own network boundary; all traffic passes through Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall enforcing org-wide policy
Real-time spend caps are set in the Cloud Billing Console — when a cap triggers, that project's agent pauses until a human resumes it
Audit trails are attributed to the specific agent, not a shared service account

slides.title: The Infrastructure Behind It

rows: 80% better price-performance than the prior generation
Argon (frontier reasoning), Flash (speed/volume), Omni (generative media), Gemma (open-weight, edge)
Down ~98% since 2024 (per a linked external source)
~500 Google Cloud customers each processed over 1 trillion tokens in the past year

slides.title: A Concrete Workflow: The Coworker Agent That Doesn't Clock Out
slides.body: Picture a finance team's coworker agent, tagged in a Google Docs comment to validate a quarterly model against live data.
bullets: It pulls figures through the BigQuery connector, cross-checks them against a saved operational report (which runs without extra token cost once saved)

It flags a discrepancy, drafts a comment back in the doc, and — per the announcement's "proactive delegation" feature — suggests which follow-up emails a human should personally send versus which it can draft itself
The job keeps running in Google's cloud after the analyst logs off for the day, and picks back up with full context the next morning across whichever device they open

slides.title: Read the ROI Numbers Skeptically
slides.body: The announcement is also, candidly, a sales pitch — dozens of customer-reported wins ("document review cut from 1 hour to 5 minutes," "conversion tripled") are stacked throughout.
bullets: Those figures are vendor- and customer-self-reported, with no disclosed measurement methodology
No GA dates, regions, or pricing/SKUs are given for the core Gemini agent itself — only that industry-specific versions (Financial Services, Legal) are in preview, others "coming soon"
A platform promising this much surface area (chat, execution, scheduling, sub-agents, memory, governance) is also a lot of attack surface and a lot that can go wrong operationally before it matures
Model-routing across two different vendors' models (Gemini and Claude) is novel, but means debugging behavior differences across providers inside one "agent"

slides.title: What's Actually New Here
bullets: A single agent interface meant to replace per-tool bots, with persistent cross-device memory and execution that survives closing your laptop
Multi-vendor model routing — Gemini and Claude today — baked into one orchestration layer, not a one-model product
Governance built in from the start: cryptographic agent identity, a dedicated network firewall for agent traffic, and billing-level spend caps that can pause a runaway agent
Treat the specific ROI percentages as marketing claims, not independently verified benchmarks, until third parties test them

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Tokens to Go Faster
posts.subtitle: A cheap draft model guesses ahead; the expensive model just checks the guesses, exactly.
posts.summary: Autoregressive LLMs normally spend one full, expensive forward pass to produce a single token. Speculative decoding has a small draft model guess several tokens ahead, then lets the big model verify all of them in one pass — accepting the ones it agrees with and provably producing the exact same output distribution as if it had generated every token itself.

slides.title: One Token Per Expensive Pass Is Wasteful
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates normally costs one full forward pass through every layer of the network — even though, at typical serving batch sizes, most of the GPU's compute sits idle waiting on memory.
bullets: Autoregressive generation: 1 forward pass → 1 token, every time
Speculative decoding verifies several guessed tokens in that same one pass
The trick: guessing is cheap, verifying several guesses at once is almost as cheap as verifying one

slides.title: Why Decoding Is Memory-Bound, Not Compute-Bound
slides.body: Generating text one token at a time means the GPU reloads and streams through every weight in the model just to compute a single next-token distribution.
bullets: At small batch sizes, that forward pass is bottlenecked on memory bandwidth — moving weights from GPU memory to compute units — not on raw FLOPs
Most of the chip's arithmetic capacity sits unused during a batch-of-1 decode step
That's the gap speculative decoding exploits: if the pass is underutilized anyway, score multiple candidate tokens in it for nearly the same cost as scoring one

slides.title: How It Actually Works
slides.body: A small, fast "draft" model generates a handful of candidate tokens on its own, cheaply and sequentially. The big "target" model then scores all of them in a single forward pass.
bullets: Draft model proposes K tokens ahead (commonly 4–8) using its own fast autoregressive generation
Target model runs one pass over the draft sequence, producing its own probability for each position — this is scoring, not generating, so it parallelizes across positions

Rejection sampling walks the K tokens left to right: accept each one the target model would plausibly have chosen too; at the first mismatch, reject it and resample that position directly from the target's own distribution
This rejection-sampling step is what makes the output provably identical in distribution to plain token-by-token decoding — it's an exact method, not a lossy shortcut

slides.title: Worked Example: Accept Four, Reject One
slides.body: Draft model proposes: "The capital of France is Paris and" (5 tokens). The target model verifies all 5 in one pass.
bullets: Target agrees with the first 4 tokens — they match what it would have sampled
Target disagrees on token 5 (the draft guessed differently than the target's own distribution would have)

Result: accept the first 4 tokens for free, discard token 5, and resample that position directly from the target model — net gain of 4 extra tokens for the price of 1 target pass plus cheap draft generation
If the draft and target disagreed immediately on token 1, the speedup for that step would be zero — you still always get at least 1 correct token

slides.title: Vanilla vs. Speculative vs. Other Sampling Tricks

rows: A different distribution — these change what gets picked, not how fast each pick happens

slides.title: When It Doesn't Help — or Actively Hurts
slides.body: Speculative decoding's payoff is entirely a function of how often the draft and target models agree.
bullets: Too weak a draft model → low acceptance rate → you're paying for draft generation that mostly gets thrown away
Too slow or large a draft model → its own overhead eats into the savings from skipping target passes
Highly predictable text (boilerplate, code completion) sees high acceptance and big wins; novel, creative, or highly uncertain generation sees low acceptance and small wins
It reduces wall-clock latency and the number of sequential passes — it does NOT reduce total FLOPs, since the target model still scores every position it's shown
Adds serving complexity: two models to deploy, keep in sync, and often share a compatible tokenizer

slides.title: The Core Trade
bullets: Speculative decoding swaps some cheap draft-model guessing for fewer expensive sequential passes through the big model
It's mathematically exact, not approximate — rejection sampling guarantees the same output distribution as plain decoding
Gains depend entirely on draft/target agreement ("acceptance rate") — there's no guaranteed speedup, only an expected one
It composes with other serving optimizations like continuous batching and KV caching, which is why most production LLM-serving stacks ship it as a standard option rather than a novelty

questions.prompt: Why is plain, one-token-at-a-time LLM decoding typically bottlenecked on memory bandwidth rather than raw compute?
options: GPUs cannot do floating point math fast enough for language models
At small batch sizes, each forward pass spends most of its time moving weights from memory rather than using available compute
Tokenizers are the slowest part of the pipeline
LLMs always run on CPUs, which lack parallelism
questions.explanation: At low batch sizes, a decode step is dominated by streaming model weights from memory, leaving most of the chip's arithmetic capacity idle. That underutilized capacity is exactly what speculative decoding puts to work by scoring multiple candidate tokens in the same pass.

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding produces the exact same output distribution as plain autoregressive decoding?
options: The draft model is always more accurate than the target model
Rejection sampling: tokens matching the target's own distribution are accepted, and the first mismatch is resampled directly from the target model
The two models are trained to produce identical outputs
Averaging the draft and target model's probabilities together
questions.explanation: The rejection-sampling step is the key correctness guarantee: every accepted token is one the target model itself would plausibly produce, and any mismatch is immediately corrected by sampling from the target's own distribution — so the method is exact, not an approximation.

questions.prompt: When does speculative decoding give the smallest speedup?
options: When generating highly predictable, repetitive text like boilerplate code
When the draft and target models frequently disagree, such as on novel or highly creative text
When the draft model is extremely fast
When batch size is very large
questions.explanation: The speedup comes from the target model accepting the draft's guesses. When draft and target frequently disagree — common on novel or highly uncertain generation — fewer tokens get accepted per round, shrinking the benefit.

posts.title: FlashProve: Proving Which AI Model Actually Answered You
posts.subtitle: Anthropic's open-source zkSNARK system lets anyone verify a reply came from committed model weights — without ever seeing those weights.
posts.summary: FlashProve is Anthropic's open-source research prototype for cryptographically proving that a specific committed model produced a given reply, without revealing the model's weights. It works, but proving costs 70-95x the GPU time of normal serving — a real research step, not yet a production tool.

slides.title: What If You Could Prove Which Model Replied?
slides.body: On November 2, 2026, Anthropic open-sourced FlashProve: a cryptographic proof system that lets anyone verify an AI reply came from a specific, committed set of model weights — without ever seeing those weights.
bullets: Built on zkSNARKs — succinct zero-knowledge cryptographic proofs
Targets a real 400B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (Llama 4 Maverick)
Apache 2.0, code on GitHub, core security properties proved in Lean 4

slides.title: You Can't Verify Which Model You Actually Got
slides.body: When you call an API, you're trusting the provider that the reply really came from the model you requested — a routing layer could silently swap in a cheaper model, or a response could be altered in transit.
bullets: No cryptographic way today to confirm 'this text came from committed weights W'
Matters for AI-pacing agreements, regulatory compliance, tamper detection, and provenance of AI-assisted work
Trust currently rests entirely on the provider's word, with no independent check

slides.title: Commit, Prove, Verify
slides.body: FlashProve splits the problem into three phases built around a zkSNARK — a proof that reveals nothing about the weights except that they produced the claimed output.
bullets: Commit (offline): provider publishes a short cryptographic commitment to the model weights; the weights themselves stay hidden
Prove (online, per request): the provider's GPU generates a proof that the committed model produced the exact output tokens for the given prompt
Verify (anyone, CPU-only): given the commitment, prompt, and reply, anyone checks the proof — no GPU, no access to weights needed
Prover cost scales with the ~17B parameters actually active per token in the MoE model, not all 400B

slides.title: Walking Through a Real Proof
slides.body: Anthropic benchmarked FlashProve on Llama 4 Maverick (400B total parameters, MoE, 4-bit weights) on a single NVIDIA H100.
bullets: Offline: committing to the weights takes ~39 minutes and the commitment stays valid for about 16 million future requests
Online: the prover generates proofs at ~110 tokens/second, producing an ~18.8 MB proof per 1,024-token window
Verify: a CPU verifier checks it in ~17 seconds on 24 threads (~21s single-threaded), downloading only ~6.5 MB of commitment data plus the proof
End result: a user with no GPU and no access to the weights can still mathematically confirm which model answered

slides.title: How FlashProve Stacks Up
Why This Isn't Production-Ready
slides.body: Anthropic is explicit that FlashProve is a research prototype, and the GitHub repo is marked 'not maintained.'
bullets: Proving overhead is still 70-95x the GPU time of normal serving — too slow and expensive for most live traffic
Only covers an integer model under greedy decoding — no floating-point or sampled (temperature > 0) generation
Context window capped at 1,024 tokens per proof
Zero-knowledge hides the weights but NOT the architecture, and side-channel leakage is explicitly out of scope
The fast C++ verifier used in practice isn't formally proven to match the Lean-verified specification

slides.title: A Real Step Toward Verifiable AI, Not a Finished Tool
bullets: FlashProve proves cryptographic verification of AI inference is practically possible, even on a real 400B-parameter MoE model
The core trick: exploit MoE sparsity so prover cost tracks active experts (~17B), not the full model (400B)
70-95x overhead means this fits audits, compliance checks, and spot-verification today — not every request
Expect proving costs to fall over time, the same way general zkSNARK tooling has over the past decade

questions.prompt: In FlashProve's zero-knowledge proof, what exactly stays hidden from the verifier?
options: Nothing — the verifier sees the full model weights
The model's weights, but not its architecture
The architecture, but not the weights
Both the prompt and the reply
questions.explanation: FlashProve's zero-knowledge property hides the model's weights behind a commitment, but the architecture (e.g., that it's a Mixture-of-Experts model with a given structure) is not hidden — only the weight values are secret.

questions.prompt: Why does FlashProve's prover cost scale with ~17B parameters instead of Llama 4 Maverick's full 400B?
options: Because it only proves a compressed, lower-quality version of the model
Because it's a Mixture-of-Experts model, and only the experts actually activated for a given token need to be proven
Because it skips proving the attention layers entirely
Because 17B is simply a hardcoded limit in the software
questions.explanation: Llama 4 Maverick is a 400B-parameter MoE model, but only ~17B parameters (the routed experts) are active per token. Since the proof only needs to cover the computation that actually ran, prover work tracks the active parameters, not the total.

questions.prompt: What is the single biggest practical barrier to using FlashProve on live production traffic today?
options: It requires revealing the model weights to every user
Proving takes roughly 70-95x the GPU time of normal serving, on top of a 1,024-token context cap
It cannot be verified without a GPU
It only works on dense models, not Mixture-of-Experts models
questions.explanation: The huge proving overhead (70-95x normal serving GPU time) plus the 1,024-token context limit mean FlashProve suits periodic audits and spot-checks far better than proving every live request.
